summary: Ionizing Lyman continuum (LyC; $λ< 912~\rm{\mathring{A}}$) radiation from low-redshift ($z \sim 0.3$) galaxies provides crucial insight into the processes that contributed to cosmic reionization. While the \textit{James Webb Space Telescope} has observed galaxies at redshifts as high as $z \sim 14$, detecting LyC beyond $z \sim 3$ is challenging due to absorption by neutral hydrogen in the intergalactic medium (IGM). Low-redshift LyC emitters (LCEs), therefore, act as proxies for their high-redshift counterparts, enabling direct measurements of LyC escape fractions with reduced IGM interference. These observations allow detailed ancillary studies of galaxy properties and the mechanisms driving ionizing photon escape, which cannot be directly observed at the Epoch of Reionization. This paper examines the capabilities of the Supernova remnants and Proxies for Re-Ionization Testbed Experiment (SPRITE) SmallSat, designed to study LyC emission from star-forming galaxies at $0.16 < z < 0.4$. SPRITE uses advanced mirror coatings and a highly sensitive far-ultraviolet imaging spectrograph, enabling it to probe LyC from galaxies that have been difficult to study with prior and existing instruments. To assess SPRITE's predicted performance in LyC studies, we select eight previously confirmed LCEs from the Low-redshift Lyman Continuum Survey as commissioning targets. Observations of these commissioning LCEs will validate SPRITE's LyC sensitivity and characterize its detection limits. This will enable the broader SPRITE low-redshift LCE survey, which will provide new constraints on the physics of LyC escape and help bridge the gap between low- and high-redshift LyC studies. SPRITE will also inform the design and scientific potential of future Lyman-UV missions, including the Habitable Worlds Observatory.

AI.tldr: The paper assesses the SPRITE SmallSat's capability to study Lyman continuum radiation from low-redshift (z~0.3) galaxies as proxies for high-redshift reionization sources, using eight confirmed LCEs as commissioning targets to validate sensitivity and inform future missions like the Habitable Worlds Observatory.
AI.motivation: Low-redshift LyC emitters serve as crucial proxies for studying cosmic reionization processes, as direct LyC detection at high redshift (z>3) is nearly impossible due to IGM absorption. Existing instruments have limited sensitivity for these studies.
AI.method: The SPRITE SmallSat, equipped with advanced mirror coatings and a far-ultraviolet imaging spectrograph, will observe eight previously confirmed LCEs from the Low-redshift Lyman Continuum Survey as commissioning targets to validate its LyC sensitivity and characterize detection limits.
AI.result: SPRITE will probe LyC from galaxies at 0.16<z<0.4 that have been difficult to study with prior instruments. Commissioning observations will validate sensitivity, enabling a broader low-redshift LCE survey to constrain LyC escape physics.
AI.conclusion: SPRITE will bridge low- and high-redshift LyC studies, provide new constraints on ionizing photon escape mechanisms, and inform the design of future Lyman-UV missions including the Habitable Worlds Observatory.

title: Revised orbital parameters of the gamma2 Velorum system
comment: 14 pages, 10 figures, and 7 tables
summary:
Context. gamma2 Velorum is the closest and visually brightest Wolf-Rayet binary system. Its eccentric orbit modulates the X-rays observed from the wind-wind interaction, and its large separation allows for spatially resolving both components.
  Aims. We aim to strengthen the constraints on gamma2 Velorum's properties and, in particular, solve the discrepancy between the eccentricity determined from the emission lines and that from the absorption lines.
  Methods. We obtained VLT/GRAVITY observations and combined them with earlier spatially-resolved data at different orbital phases.
  Results. Strong constraints on all orbital parameters were determined and, in particular, we find that e=0.322, close to what was derived from the emission lines. The X-ray light curve declines as s to power -3 after periastron, where s is the separation of the two stars, but its modulation is likely affected by absorption and occultation of the X-ray emitting region at other orbital phases. We find that previous discrepancies in the reddening value can be traced to a brighter K-band magnitude than that predicted by the WR wind models. We conclude E(B-V)=0.02+-0.02 mag. Our now more precise mass and radius values combined with previously determined effective temperatures provide very strong constraints on evolutionary models. The closest match for the O-star is provided by an initial mass M=28.7 Mo rotationally mixed model and a M=32 Mo model for the WR star, with negligible accretion onto the O-star during the WR progenitor's Roche Lobe overflow phase. However, the temperature of the O star is higher and the mass of the WR star is found to be smaller than predicted by the evolutionary tracks for the current epoch, consistent with the well-known "mass-discrepancy problem" in massive stars.

AI.tldr: γ² Velorum, the closest Wolf-Rayet binary, is analyzed using VLT/GRAVITY and earlier spatially-resolved data. Orbital parameters are tightly constrained (e=0.322), resolving eccentricity discrepancies. The X-ray light curve scales as s⁻³ post-periastron but is affected by absorption/occultation. Reddening E(B-V)=0.02±0.02 mag. Evolutionary models favor a 28.7 M⊙ rotationally-mixed O-star and 32 M⊙ WR star with negligible Roche Lobe overflow accretion, though the mass-discrepancy problem persists.
AI.motivation: To strengthen constraints on γ² Velorum's properties and resolve the discrepancy between eccentricities derived from emission lines versus absorption lines.
AI.method: VLT/GRAVITY interferometric observations combined with earlier spatially-resolved data across multiple orbital phases.
AI.result: Orbital eccentricity e=0.322 (consistent with emission-line values); X-ray light curve declines as s⁻³ post-periastron; reddening E(B-V)=0.02±0.02 mag; O-star best fit: 28.7 M⊙ rotationally-mixed model, WR star: 32 M⊙ model.
AI.conclusion: The mass-discrepancy problem persists (higher O-star temperature, lower WR mass than evolutionary tracks predict); negligible accretion during Roche Lobe overflow phase; improved constraints on orbital and stellar parameters.

title: Cm-wavelength Studies of Molecular Gas and Star Formation at High Redshift with the SKA
comment: Published in Advancing Astrophysics with the SKA II (AASKAII), 2026(arXiv:2606.20366). Report-no: AASKAII/RanWang01. Advancing Astrophysics with the SKA II (AASKAII) outlines the transformative scientific advances that will be enabled by the SKA telescopes
summary: The Square Kilometre Array will be a revolutionary instrument for the study of gas in the distant Universe. At frequencies below ~50 GHz, observations of redshifted emission from low-J transitions of CO, HCN, HCO+, and HNC, etc. provide insight into the kinematics and mass budget of the cold, dense star-forming gas in galaxies. Over the past decade, sensitive imaging using ALMA has detected and resolved the redshifted high-J molecular CO line emission and far-infrared fine structure lines in samples of galaxies over a wide redshift range, shedding light on active star-formation processes at the early epoch of galaxy evolution. In recent years, increasing numbers of young galaxies at high redshift are discovered by JWST, which significantly improved our knowledge of different galaxy populations across cosmic time. In this updated chapter of the SKA science book, we would like to highlight the importance of studies of the low-J molecular lines in high-z galaxies using SKA toward high frequencies, discussing the request of frequency coverage beyond 15 GHz and emphasizing its crucial role in exploring the cold molecular gas content in the young galaxy populations in the early universe and investigating the regions of active-star formation using molecular CO and various dense gas tracers.

AI.tldr: This SKA science book chapter emphasizes the importance of low-J molecular line observations (CO, HCN, HCO+, HNC) at frequencies >15 GHz with SKA to study cold molecular gas and star formation in high-redshift galaxies, complementing ALMA's high-J CO and JWST's discoveries of young galaxies.
AI.motivation: To highlight the need for SKA's frequency coverage beyond 15 GHz to enable low-J molecular line studies of cold gas in high-z galaxies, which is critical for understanding gas kinematics, mass budgets, and star formation in young galaxy populations discovered by JWST, complementing ALMA's high-J observations.
AI.method: Review of low-J molecular transitions (CO, HCN, HCO+, HNC) as tracers of cold dense star-forming gas; analysis of SKA's required frequency coverage (>15 GHz) for observing redshifted lines in high-z galaxies, building on insights from ALMA (high-J CO, far-infrared fine structure lines) and JWST (galaxy population discoveries).
AI.result: Low-J molecular line observations with SKA at high frequencies (>15 GHz) are crucial for probing cold molecular gas content and active star-forming regions in early-universe galaxy populations, filling a gap left by ALMA's high-J and far-infrared tracers.
AI.conclusion: SKA's extended frequency coverage beyond 15 GHz is essential for advancing our understanding of cold gas and star formation in high-redshift galaxies, particularly for the young galaxy populations unveiled by JWST.

title: Astrochemical Study of Early Embedded Disks
comment: Accepted for publication in Frontiers in Astronomy and Space Sciences
summary: The question of how our planet was formed and, more generally, how a planetary system forms is fundamental and has been addressed in a broad range of research domains. However, we still lack a comprehensive understanding of the basic aspects of the process of star and planet formation. In particular, the challenge of measuring the mass and chemical composition of young protostellar disks has, so far, hampered a meaningful comparison with observed exoplanet populations. This will become critical in the near future to interpret the results of European space missions, such as Ariel, which will yield a comprehensive inventory of exoplanetary masses and chemical compositions. Building on recent developments in astrochemistry and data science, this perspective explores future research avenues for the study of young planet-forming disks and introduces the project "Astrochemical Study of Early Embedded Disks" (iSEEDs). By integrating machine learning and data mining with astrochemistry, iSEEDs provides a robust framework to systematically extract the physical conditions and molecular abundances hidden within high-resolution datasets of protostellar environments.

AI.tldr: This perspective discusses the challenge of measuring mass and chemical composition of young protostellar disks to compare with exoplanet populations, and introduces the iSEEDs project which integrates machine learning and data mining with astrochemistry to systematically extract physical conditions and molecular abundances from high-resolution protostellar datasets.
AI.motivation: We lack a comprehensive understanding of star and planet formation, particularly in measuring the mass and chemical composition of young protostellar disks, which hampers meaningful comparison with observed exoplanet populations and will be critical for interpreting results from upcoming European space missions like Ariel.
AI.method: Building on recent developments in astrochemistry and data science, the iSEEDs project integrates machine learning and data mining with astrochemistry to provide a robust framework for systematically extracting physical conditions and molecular abundances from high-resolution datasets of protostellar environments.
AI.result: A robust framework (iSEEDs) is introduced that enables systematic extraction of physical conditions and molecular abundances hidden within high-resolution protostellar datasets, bridging the gap between protostellar disk measurements and exoplanet population studies.
AI.conclusion: The iSEEDs project offers a promising avenue for future research on young planet-forming disks, enabling meaningful comparisons with exoplanet populations and supporting the interpretation of data from upcoming missions like Ariel.

title: Search for Seeds of The Cradle of Stars: Study of The Evolution From Atomic to Molecular Hydrogen Clouds with 1000 AU Scale Resolution
comment: Published in Advancing Astrophysics with the SKA II (AASKAII), 2026 (arXiv:2606.20366). Report-no:AASKAII/Yamamoto01. Advancing Astrophysics with the SKA II (AASKAII) outlines the transformative scientific advances that will be enabled by the SKA telescopes
summary: The aim of this science case for SKA1-Mid is to elucidate the spatial and velocity structure of the Cold Neutral Medium (CNM) on scales below the Field length, thereby elucidating the physical processes that govern CNM structure formation and its role in the earliest stages of molecular cloud formation. This goal will be achieved through a unique observational combination of several-arcsecond angular resolution, high velocity resolution, and unprecedented surface-brightness sensitivity. These observations will reveal the characteristic size, morphology, velocity structure, and internal dynamics of CNM clumps, and will directly connect such structures to the earliest phases of the atomic to molecular transition. Full-polarization observations with SKA1-Mid will also enable emission-based Zeeman measurements of the CNM, allowing the magnetic field strength to be mapped and opening a new window on the role of magnetic fields in CNM formation and evolution. In particular, this will make it possible to determine whether magnetic fields primarily inhibit fragmentation by supporting the gas against compression, or instead guide anisotropic condensation and promote the development of small-scale CNM structure through thermal instability. In combination with interferometric spatial filtering and high spectral resolution, SKA1-Mid will selectively trace the CNM and robustly identify individual clumps in both position and velocity space. These capabilities will provide decisive tests of thermal instability and the two-phase turbulence model, and will establish a new observational foundation for understanding how molecular clouds emerge from the multi-phase atomic interstellar medium.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a science case for using SKA1-Mid to study the Cold Neutral Medium (CNM) at sub-Field-length scales, combining arcsecond angular resolution, high velocity resolution, and superior surface-brightness sensitivity to resolve CNM clump structure, dynamics, and magnetic fields via Zeeman measurements, thereby testing thermal instability models and the atomic-to-molecular transition in the interstellar medium.
AI.motivation: To elucidate the spatial and velocity structure of the Cold Neutral Medium (CNM) on scales below the Field length and understand the physical processes governing CNM structure formation and its role in the earliest stages of molecular cloud formation.
AI.method: SKA1-Mid observations combining several-arcsecond angular resolution, high velocity resolution, and unprecedented surface-brightness sensitivity, along with full-polarization observations for emission-based Zeeman measurements of magnetic field strength.
AI.result: Will reveal the characteristic size, morphology, velocity structure, and internal dynamics of CNM clumps; directly connect such structures to the atomic-to-molecular transition; map magnetic field strength; and determine whether magnetic fields inhibit fragmentation or guide anisotropic condensation via thermal instability.
AI.conclusion: These capabilities will provide decisive tests of thermal instability and the two-phase turbulence model, establishing a new observational foundation for understanding how molecular clouds emerge from the multi-phase atomic interstellar medium.

title: Unveiling Complex Chemistry in Planet-forming Disks with the SKAO
comment: Published in Advancing Astrophysics with the SKA II (AASKAII), 2026 (arXiv:2606.20366). Report-no:AASKAII/Podio01. Advancing Astrophysics with the SKA II (AASKAII) outlines the transformative scientific advances that will be enabled by the SKA telescopes
summary: The chemical composition of planets is inherited from that of the natal protoplanetary disk at the time of planet formation. In recent years, we have made huge progress in characterizing disk chemistry. (Sub-)millimeter interferometers, such as ALMA, allowed us to detect emission lines from simple to complex organic molecules and to probe their radial and vertical distribution in disks. On the other hand, JWST has started to unveil the composition of disk ices, and line emission from the innermost disk regions. The advent of SKA will open new domains in the field, by observing emission lines from heavier molecules including heavy carbon chains and rings, and prebiotic molecules with peak emission in the cm range. Moreover, SKA will probe molecular emission from regions which are obscured by dust opacity at mm wavelengths, hence from the disk midplane, and often from the inner 30 au region. These observations will constrain the initial conditions for disk evolution and planet formation, allowing us to predict the chemical composition of the forming planets and their atmospheres. Comparison with forthcoming results on exoplanet atmospheres and on the chemistry of pristine bodies in the Solar System will provide new hints on the origin and evolution of planetary systems including our own.

AI.tldr: This paper reviews how disk chemistry (from ALMA, JWST, and the future SKA) constrains the chemical composition of forming planets, linking protoplanetary disk observations to exoplanet atmospheres and Solar System bodies.
AI.motivation: Understanding the chemical composition of planets requires knowledge of the natal protoplanetary disk chemistry at the time of planet formation. Recent observational advances now make it possible to link disk chemistry to planetary compositions.
AI.method: The authors review observational progress from (sub-)millimeter interferometers (ALMA) for molecular line emission, JWST for disk ices and inner disk lines, and discuss the future capabilities of SKA to observe heavier molecules, prebiotic species, and dust-obscured midplane/inner regions.
AI.result: ALMA has enabled detection of simple to complex organic molecules and their spatial distribution; JWST reveals ices and inner-disk emission; SKA will probe heavy carbon chains, rings, prebiotic molecules in the cm range, and regions obscured at mm wavelengths (midplane, inner 30 au).
AI.conclusion: These observations will constrain initial conditions for planet formation and predict planetary compositions. Comparison with exoplanet atmosphere data and Solar System pristine bodies will elucidate the origin and evolution of planetary systems.

title: Extended Structure in E+A Galaxies Via Image Stacking
comment: 18 pages, 14 figures
summary: Small-scale interactions such as minor mergers, flybys and harassment are considered common driving mechanisms that can both initiate and quench star-forming processes within post-starburst (PSB) galaxies. PSBs have been linked to disturbed morphologies and faint tidal features in numerous works. We aim to independently study these features in E+A galaxies found in the Galaxy and Mass Assembly Fourth Data Release (GAMA DR4). Using image stacking techniques, we derive the averaged radial surface brightness profiles of E+A image stacks alongside the Sérsic parameters that best fit these profiles. These E+A stacks consist of 57 images extracted from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) in g, r & i bands. The E+A stacks are shown to have brighter extended regions than similar non-PSB galaxies, which is indicative of faint tidal features that could be caused by small-scale interactions. Additionally, we make use of Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) Legacy Survey imaging, which is deeper than SDSS, to further support our conclusions and find that the Legacy Survey images independently strengthen the evidence for excess light at extended radii relative to the comparison samples. We discuss these findings in the context of future surveys such as the Vera C. Rubin Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST) survey.

AI.tldr: Using image stacking of 57 SDSS E+A (post-starburst) galaxies from GAMA DR4, the study finds these galaxies exhibit brighter extended regions and excess light at large radii compared to non-PSB galaxies, indicative of faint tidal features from small-scale interactions (mergers, flybys, harassment). Deeper DESI Legacy Survey imaging independently confirms these results. Findings are discussed in context of future LSST surveys.
AI.motivation: To independently investigate whether E+A (post-starburst) galaxies show disturbed morphologies and faint tidal features indicative of small-scale interactions (minor mergers, flybys, harassment) that may drive their starburst-quenching cycles.
AI.method: Image stacking of 57 E+A galaxies from GAMA DR4 with SDSS g, r, i band images; extraction of averaged radial surface brightness profiles; fitting Sérsic profiles to stacks; comparison to non-PSB galaxy stacks; validation using deeper DESI Legacy Survey imaging.
AI.result: E+A stacks exhibit brighter extended regions and excess light at large radii compared to non-PSB galaxy stacks. These faint tidal features are consistent with signatures of small-scale interactions. DESI Legacy Survey data independently corroborate these findings.
AI.conclusion: E+A galaxies show excess extended emission likely arising from tidal features due to small-scale interactions, supporting the role of such processes in PSB evolution. Future deep surveys like LSST will further elucidate these features.

title: Theoretical determination of the binding energies of methanol and related species onto amorphous solid water ice
comment: Resubmitted to AAS Journals following revision
summary: The formation and survival of complex organic molecules (COMs) in cold interstellar environments depends on their interactions with icy dust grain surfaces. Methanol, a key COM detected in cold cores and protoplanetary disks, is believed to form on amorphous solid water (ASW) through surface reactions and reside there until it is desorbed into the gas phase. We present a theoretical study of the binding energies (BEs) of methanol and its photolysis-derived species on ASW clusters by means of dispersion-corrected density functional theory (DFT) using a refined protocol implemented in the Binding Energy Evaluation Platform (BEEP). Molecules capable of hydrogen bonding, such as H2O, CH3OH, HCOOH, and OH, exhibit high BEs and broad BE distributions that reflect the structural heterogeneity of the ASW surface. In contrast, weakly interacting volatiles including CO, CO2, CH4, and CH3 display narrower distributions dominated by dispersion interactions. Open-shell radicals such as CH2OH and OH bind more strongly than HCO and CH3 due to their ability to form directional hydrogen bonds. Incorporation of our BEs into an astrochemical model, in conjunction with a recalculation of the pre-exponential factor using transition state theory, demonstrates the sensitivity of model results to the method of calculation of the grain-surface reaction rates. The new approach generally predicts a higher abundance of radicals on the ice that are key reactants for the formation of COMs when surface diffusion is assumed to be efficient. These findings emphasize the importance of incorporating BEs that have been determined in a self-consistent manner into astrochemical models, and provide reliable theoretical benchmarks for species with limited experimental data.

AI.tldr: This study uses DFT to compute binding energies of methanol and its photolysis-derived species on amorphous solid water clusters, finding that hydrogen-bonding species have high and broad BE distributions while weakly interacting species have narrow dispersion-dominated distributions. Incorporating these self-consistent BEs into astrochemical models affects predicted radical abundances on ice surfaces, highlighting the importance of reliable theoretical benchmarks for COM formation modeling.
AI.motivation: To understand the formation and survival of complex organic molecules (COMs) in cold interstellar environments, accurate binding energies of methanol and its photolysis products on icy dust grain surfaces are needed, as these govern surface reactions and desorption processes in astrochemical models.
AI.method: Dispersion-corrected density functional theory (DFT) calculations using a refined protocol implemented in the Binding Energy Evaluation Platform (BEEP) on amorphous solid water (ASW) clusters; incorporation of calculated BEs into an astrochemical model with recalculated pre-exponential factors using transition state theory.
AI.result: Hydrogen-bonding species (H2O, CH3OH, HCOOH, OH) exhibit high BEs with broad distributions reflecting ASW surface heterogeneity; weakly interacting volatiles (CO, CO2, CH4, CH3) show narrow dispersion-dominated distributions; open-shell radicals (CH2OH, OH) bind more strongly than HCO and CH3; the new model predicts higher radical abundances on ice when surface diffusion is efficient.
AI.conclusion: Self-consistently determined binding energies are critical for accurate astrochemical modeling, and the DFT-based theoretical benchmarks provide reliable reference data for species with limited experimental measurements.

title: SKA VLBI survey of the Southern sky for astrometry, geodesy, and astrophysics
comment: Published in Advancing Astrophysics with the SKA II (AASKAII), 2026 (arXiv:2606.20366). Report-no:AASKAII/MingHuiXu01
summary: The development of SKA will open the opportunity to run dedicated VLBI surveys of the Southern sky and observe sources not visible at radio telescopes located in the Northern hemisphere. These surveys will allow for doing geodesy with a Southern hemisphere-centered network, increase the density of compact radio sources that can be used as calibrators, further extend the celestial reference frame to deep south, and facilitate high-precision differential astrometry for a wide range of applications. Achieving a deep completeness level and determining the parsec-scale properties of extragalactic radio sources is crucial for multi-wavelength and multi-messenger astrophysics. This includes supporting Cherenkov and neutrino telescope science cases, as well as joint VLBI-Gaia studies of active galaxies.

AI.tldr: The paper discusses how the SKA will enable Southern-hemisphere VLBI surveys, improving geodesy, calibrator source density, celestial reference frames, and differential astrometry, while supporting multi-messenger astrophysics including Cherenkov/neutrino telescopes and VLBI-Gaia studies.
AI.motivation: To leverage SKA's capabilities for dedicated VLBI surveys of the Southern sky, which has been poorly covered by Northern-hemisphere-dominated radio telescopes, and to enable high-precision astrometry and geodesy for the Southern celestial hemisphere.
AI.method: The paper outlines the concept of using SKA for VLBI observations targeting Southern sky sources, focusing on survey design for deep completeness, parsec-scale source characterization, and integration with multi-wavelength/multi-messenger facilities.
AI.result: Expected outcomes include improved Southern-hemisphere geodesy, increased density of compact radio calibrators, extension of the celestial reference frame to the deep south, and enabling high-precision differential astrometry.
AI.conclusion: SKA-based VLBI surveys will be critical for multi-wavelength and multi-messenger astrophysics, supporting Cherenkov/neutrino telescope science and joint VLBI-Gaia studies of active galactic nuclei.

title: NO molecule in massive star forming regions
summary: Context. Among diatomic molecules composed of the abundant elements C, N and O, NO has been detected far less than the well studied CN and CO, making it a crucial yet under-observed component in nitrogen-containing chemical networks. NO was thought to serve as a potential tracer of shocks, as evidenced with orders abundance enhancements reported in literature. Aims. Large-sample observations for NO molecule in widespread interstellar environments are needed to confirm if the enhancement of NO is due to shock chemistry or not. Methods. Single-point survey for NO lines around 150 GHz was carried out by Arizona Radio Observatory 12-meter telescope towards a sample of 36 massive star forming regions containing SiO emission, which include three evolutionary stages: 4 IRDCs, 6 protostars and 26 H II regions. Results. The NO emission was detected in 28 sources with a detection rate of 78%. Beam-averaged NO column densities and abundances relative to H2 were derived from integrated intensities of two main hyperfine lines. Correlations between NO and SiO in integrated intensity and relative abundance are similar to the corresponding correlations of c-C3H2, indicating that NO enrichment may not significantly involve pronounced shock activities, which coincides with the trend in line widths: NO is close to c-C3H2, both smaller than H2CO and far smaller than SiO. Conclusions. Observational evidence does not strongly support significant NO enhancement by shock chemistry in the observed sources, indicating that the formation of NO does not necessarily require shocks.

AI.tldr: This paper surveys NO emission around 150 GHz towards 36 massive star-forming regions with SiO emission, detecting NO in 78% of sources. Correlations with SiO and c-C3H2, along with line width comparisons, suggest NO enhancement is not primarily driven by shock chemistry, contrary to earlier assumptions.
AI.motivation: NO is under-observed compared to CN and CO despite being a key component in nitrogen-containing chemical networks. Previous studies reported orders-of-magnitude abundance enhancements of NO attributed to shocks, but large-sample observations across diverse interstellar environments were lacking to confirm this connection.
AI.method: Single-point survey of NO lines near 150 GHz using the Arizona Radio Observatory 12-meter telescope toward 36 massive star-forming regions exhibiting SiO emission, spanning three evolutionary stages: 4 infrared dark clouds (IRDCs), 6 protostars, and 26 H II regions. Beam-averaged NO column densities and abundances relative to H2 were derived from integrated intensities of two main hyperfine lines.
AI.result: NO detected in 28/36 sources (78% detection rate). Correlations between NO and SiO in integrated intensity and relative abundance resemble those of c-C3H2, not SiO. Line widths: NO ≈ c-C3H2 < H2CO << SiO, indicating NO is not closely linked to shock-tracing SiO.
AI.conclusion: Observational evidence does not strongly support significant NO enhancement by shock chemistry. NO formation does not necessarily require shocks, suggesting alternative chemical pathways dominate in these regions.

title: Semi-empirical Predictions for Ultra-deep Radio Counts of Star-forming Galaxies with the SKAO
comment: Published in Advancing Astrophysics with the SKAII (AASKAII), 2026(arXiv:2606.20366). Report-no:AASKAII/Giulietti01. Advancing Astrophysics with the SKAII (AASKAII) outlines the transformative scientific advances that will be enabled by the SKA telescopes
summary: Star-forming galaxies (SFGs) dominate the faint radio sky at flux densities below 0.1 mJy. Identifying these systems through a multiwavelength approach is essential to tracing the cosmic history of star formation. Upcoming surveys with the Square Kilometre Array Observatory (SKAO) in its AA4 configuration for the Mid array will probe these faint populations, offering unprecedented insights into the star formation activity of galaxies across cosmic time. Semi-empirical models, built on minimal assumptions and empirical galaxy relations, provide an efficient framework to study galaxy evolution using recent radio and optical/near-infrared (NIR) data. We developed SEMPER (Semi-EMPirical model for Extragalactic Radio emission) to predict the radio luminosity functions and number counts of SFGs. SEMPER combines redshift-dependent stellar mass functions from deep NIR surveys with empirical relations such as the galaxy main sequence and the IR/radio correlation, to characterise the radio properties of massive, high-redshift galaxies. The model shows excellent agreement with recent deep radio observations and naturally predicts a substantial population of massive, dust-obscured galaxies already in place at early epochs. In this chapter, we extend the SEMPER framework to SKA surveys by including an evolving starburst fraction and computing differential number counts at 1.4 GHz for both lensed and unlensed SFGs. Furthermore, we predict the cosmic star formation rate density (SFRD) traced by radio-emitting galaxies up to $z\approx10$. Our results show that SKA surveys will probe the faintest flux-density regimes, dominated by galaxies powered by star formation, and that <20 hours of SKA-Mid Band 2 observations will recover at least $\approx$20% of the total SFRD predicted by SEMPER, including contributions from optically/NIR-dark systems up to $z\approx 6$.

AI.tldr: SEMPER is a semi-empirical model predicting radio emission from star-forming galaxies, showing that <20 hours of SKA-Mid Band 2 observations will recover ~20% of the cosmic star formation rate density up to z≈6.
AI.motivation: To develop a predictive framework for interpreting upcoming SKA surveys of faint star-forming galaxies, and to quantify how much cosmic star formation history these surveys can recover.
AI.method: SEMPER combines redshift-dependent stellar mass functions from deep NIR surveys with empirical galaxy relations (galaxy main sequence, IR/radio correlation). The model includes an evolving starburst fraction and computes differential number counts at 1.4 GHz for both lensed and unlensed SFGs.
AI.result: The model agrees well with deep radio observations, predicts a substantial population of massive dust-obscured galaxies at early epochs, and shows SKA-Mid Band 2 observations (<20 hours) will recover ≥20% of the total predicted SFRD, including optically/NIR-dark systems up to z≈6.
AI.conclusion: SKA surveys will probe the faintest flux-density regimes dominated by star-forming galaxies, and SEMPER provides the framework to interpret these surveys and trace cosmic star formation history.

title: Validating the ICCF-Cut Method with Simultaneous Photometric and Spectroscopic H$α$ Reverberation Mapping of NGC 4151 and UGC 3374
comment: 24 pages, 15 figures, 2 tables. Accepted for publication in ApJ
summary: Photometric reverberation mapping (RM) provides an efficient alternative to spectroscopic RM for probing the broad-line region (BLR) sizes in AGNs. In our previous work, we proposed the ICCF-Cut method, which extracts H$α$ emission-line variability from broadband photometric light curves and measures the lags to estimate the BLR sizes. To further assess the reliability of this method, we conduct simultaneous photometric and spectroscopic monitoring of two nearby Seyfert galaxies, NGC 4151 and UGC 3374, over multiple observing seasons using the Lijiang 2.4 m telescope. By directly comparing the photometric and spectroscopic RM results in each season, we find that the extracted H$α$ light curves using the ICCF-Cut method closely resemble those derived from spectroscopy. The photometric H$α$ lags are also generally consistent with the spectroscopic H$α$ lags within the uncertainties. For several seasons where the photometric H$α$ lags are slightly underestimated, we find that the discrepancy may be caused by residual He\,\textsc{i} contamination in the extracted H$α$ light curves. After correcting for this contamination, the photometric lag measurements become more consistent with the spectroscopic results. We further explore the performance of the ICCF-Cut method using the simulated light curves with different filter bandwidths. For our observational and simulated cases, the method can successfully recover the emission-line variability and lag measurements broadly consistent with the spectroscopic results. This provides further support for the applicability of the ICCF-Cut method in photometric RM.

AI.tldr: The ICCF-Cut method for photometric reverberation mapping is tested on NGC 4151 and UGC 3374 via simultaneous photometric and spectroscopic monitoring. Extracted Hα light curves and lags generally agree with spectroscopic results, with minor discrepancies due to He I contamination. Simulations confirm broad reliability of the method.
AI.motivation: To assess the reliability of the ICCF-Cut method for photometric reverberation mapping by directly comparing its photometric Hα lag measurements with simultaneous spectroscopic results from two Seyfert galaxies over multiple seasons.
AI.method: Simultaneous photometric and spectroscopic monitoring of NGC 4151 and UGC 3374 using the Lijiang 2.4 m telescope; application of the ICCF-Cut method to extract Hα emission-line variability from broadband photometric light curves; comparison of photometric and spectroscopic lags; correction for He I contamination; simulation with varying filter bandwidths.
AI.result: Photometric Hα light curves and lags generally agree with spectroscopic results within uncertainties. Slight underestimation in some seasons is attributed to residual He I contamination; correction yields better consistency. Simulated light curves confirm method recovers lags broadly consistent with spectroscopy.
AI.conclusion: The ICCF-Cut method is a reliable tool for photometric reverberation mapping, providing broadly consistent BLR size estimates compared to spectroscopy, with careful treatment of contaminating lines needed for optimal accuracy.

title: Feeding and Feedback in Dwarf Galaxies (FeeD) -- I. Evidence of nuclear ultra-fast and galaxy-scale outflows in the dwarf galaxy Arp 151
comment: 4 pages, 3 figures, Accepted for publication in A&A Letters
summary: Feeding and feedback regulated by supermassive black holes (SMBHs) play a central role in galaxy growth and evolution, yet these processes remain poorly understood in low-mass galaxies. In particular, the presence, properties, and role of ultra-fast nuclear outflows (UFOs) in low-mass galaxy systems are largely unexplored. We analyze available NuSTAR X-ray observations of Arp 151 and find a possible evidence ($\sim 2σ$ confidence) for a fast outflow with a velocity of $\sim0.18c$ from the central BH. Furthermore, we have also detected an optical galaxy-scale outflow in MaNGA Integral Field Unit data. The estimated nuclear and galaxy-scale mass outflow rates are $\sim0.015$ $M_\odot$/yr from {\it NuSTAR} and $\sim0.43$ $M_\odot$/yr from MaNGA, respectively. Our estimates suggest that such outflows may significantly regulate the feedback process in the galaxy. Comparing the kinetics of the UFO and the galaxy-scale outflow indicates that they are in the momentum-conserving phase. This tentative detection implies that dwarf galaxies are also able to generate UFOs, which so far have been detected in massive galaxies. Thus, the AGN feedback may also be important for the evolution of the dwarf galaxies.

AI.tldr: This paper presents tentative evidence (∼2σ) for an ultra-fast outflow (UFO) at ~0.18c from the SMBH in the low-mass galaxy Arp 151, detected via NuSTAR X-ray observations, alongside an optical galaxy-scale outflow from MaNGA. The estimated mass outflow rates (~0.015 M⊙/yr nuclear, ~0.43 M⊙/yr galaxy-scale) suggest the outflows are in a momentum-conserving phase and may significantly regulate feedback, indicating that UFOs—previously only seen in massive galaxies—also occur in dwarf galaxies, making AGN feedback potentially important for their evolution.
AI.motivation: SMBH-driven feeding and feedback are central to galaxy evolution but poorly understood in low-mass galaxies, and the role of ultra-fast nuclear outflows (UFOs) in such systems is largely unexplored.
AI.method: Analysis of NuSTAR X-ray observations of Arp 151 for nuclear outflow signatures (∼2σ confidence), combined with optical galaxy-scale outflow detection from MaNGA Integral Field Unit data.
AI.result: Possible UFO detection at ~0.18c; nuclear mass outflow rate ~0.015 M⊙/yr; galaxy-scale outflow rate ~0.43 M⊙/yr; outflows appear to be in a momentum-conserving phase.
AI.conclusion: Dwarf galaxies can generate UFOs, previously observed only in massive galaxies, implying AGN feedback may also be important for dwarf galaxy evolution.

title: Probing outflow physics through CH$_3$CN and CH$_3$OH chemistry
summary: Chemical correlations between molecules provide powerful diagnostics to probe the physical conditions of protostellar outflows. In particular, the relationship between methanol (CH$_3$OH) and methyl cyanide (CH$_3$CN) offers a promising tool to investigate the chemistry and irradiation environment of shocked gas. In this Letter, we use the CH$_3$OH/CH$_3$CN abundance ratio to constrain the physical properties of the outflow driven by the Class 0 protostar S68N using ALMA Band 3 and Band 6 observations. Assuming local thermodynamic equilibrium (LTE), we derive excitation temperatures of 50-60 K and column densities of 2-3$\times$10$^{13}$ cm$^{-2}$ for CH$_3$CN and 3-5$\times$10$^{15}$ cm$^{-2}$ for CH$_3$OH. The resulting CH$_3$OH/CH$_3$CN abundance ratio is nearly constant along the outflow, with values of $\sim$100-200, similar to those found in other protostellar environments. Using an up-to-date astrochemical model, we test whether gas-phase formation of CH$_3$CN can account for the observed ratios. We find that they are reproduced only by assuming enhanced cosmic-ray ionization rates $ζ_{\rm CR}$ up to $\sim$10$^{-14}$ s$^{-1}$. These results suggest that the CH$_3$OH-CH$_3$CN correlation can be used as a probe of the irradiation conditions in protostellar outflows. Further studies are required to explore the possible contribution of grain-surface formation of CH$_3$CN which could lead to a lower $ζ_{\rm CR}$ and to extend the analysis to a larger sample of sources.

AI.tldr: This study uses ALMA observations to measure CH₃OH/CH₃CN abundance ratios (~100-200) in the S68N protostellar outflow, finding that the observed ratios can only be reproduced by astrochemical models assuming enhanced cosmic-ray ionization rates (ζCR ~ 10⁻¹⁴ s⁻¹), suggesting this molecular ratio can probe irradiation conditions in protostellar outflows.
AI.motivation: Chemical correlations between molecules, particularly CH₃OH and CH₃CN, offer a promising diagnostic tool to investigate the chemistry and irradiation environment of shocked gas in protostellar outflows, motivating a quantitative test of this approach.
AI.method: ALMA Band 3 and Band 6 observations of the Class 0 protostar S68N outflow; LTE analysis to derive excitation temperatures (50-60 K) and column densities for CH₃CN (2-3×10¹³ cm⁻²) and CH₃OH (3-5×10¹⁵ cm⁻²); astrochemical modeling to test gas-phase CH₃CN formation under varying cosmic-ray ionization rates.
AI.result: CH₃OH/CH₃CN abundance ratio is nearly constant along the outflow at ~100-200, similar to other protostellar environments; models reproduce these ratios only when assuming enhanced cosmic-ray ionization rates up to ζCR ~ 10⁻¹⁴ s⁻¹.
AI.conclusion: The CH₃OH-CH₃CN correlation can serve as a probe of irradiation conditions in protostellar outflows; further studies should investigate grain-surface CH₃CN formation and extend the analysis to a larger sample.

title: HI Galaxy Science with the SKA
comment: Published in Advancing Astrophysics with the SKA II (AASKAII), 2026 (arXiv:2606.20366). Report-no:AASKAII/JingWang01. Advancing Astrophysics with the SKA II (AASKAII) outlines the transformative scientific advances that will be enabled by the SKA telescopes
summary: This chapter introduces the contributions of the HI galaxy science in this volume reviewing the latest developments and urgent questions in HI galaxy science, providing guiding principles for a layered set of future key science projects. The key science will include: a complete censuses of HI morphologies and kinematics at sub-kpc and 1 km/s resolution within and around galaxies in the nearby Universe; a measurement of the cosmic HI mass density and HI mass function evolution at least up to z~1; an improved understanding of the Universe at z>1, particularly the balance between cold molecular and cool atomic gas. We also provide a view of the synergistic multi-wavelength surveys available in 2028+ in the southern hemisphere. This effort will improve our understanding of the baryon cycle across a significant fraction of the cosmic history, including the processes of gas accretion, consumption and removal as well as AGN and star formation feedback. Based on these science goals, the earlier proposed three-tiered survey strategy remains, but survey parameters and predictions are adjusted according to AA* and AA4 developments. This chapter is an update of the earlier "Advancing Astrophysics with the Square Kilometre Array" chapter 'HI Science with the SKA' by Staveley-Smith & Oosterloo.

AI.tldr: This chapter updates HI galaxy science goals for the SKA, focusing on high-resolution HI morphologies/kinematics in the nearby Universe, cosmic HI mass density evolution up to z~1, and understanding cold gas at z>1. It maintains a three-tiered survey strategy with updated parameters based on AA* and AA4 developments.
AI.motivation: To review the latest developments and urgent questions in HI galaxy science, providing guiding principles for future key science projects that improve our understanding of the baryon cycle across cosmic history.
AI.method: A layered three-tiered survey strategy with updated parameters based on AA* and AA4 developments, combined with synergistic multi-wavelength surveys available in the southern hemisphere after 2028.
AI.result: Key science includes: complete censuses of HI morphologies/kinematics at sub-kpc and 1 km/s resolution in the nearby Universe; measurement of cosmic HI mass density and HI mass function evolution up to z~1; improved understanding of the cold molecular vs. cool atomic gas balance at z>1.
AI.conclusion: The proposed HI science program will improve understanding of the baryon cycle, including gas accretion, consumption, removal, and AGN/star formation feedback across a significant fraction of cosmic history.

title: Unveiling the roles of thermal and nonthermal processes in the ISM & IGM structure formation and evolution of galaxies with SKAO
comment: Published in Advancing Astrophysics with the SKA II (AASKAII), 2026 (arXiv:2026.20366). Report-no: AASKAII/Tabatabaei01. Advancing Astrophysics with the SKA II (AASKAII) outlines the transformative scientific advances that will be enabled by the SKA telescopes
summary: Investigating the thermal and nonthermal processes in the interstellar medium (ISM) and intergalactic medium (IGM) is vital to understanding the evolution of galaxies over cosmic time. Resolved observations with SKA pathfinders show that the nonthermal processes, in which magnetic fields and cosmic rays are involved, can decelerate the formation of massive stars in strongly magnetized regions in nearby galaxies. They can also contribute to the onset of winds and outflows in galaxies. The effects of these processes are stronger at higher redshifts as a result of star formation activities. The SKA Observatory will allow a major breakthrough by mapping the thermal and nonthermal processes in distant universe galaxies, shedding light on the role of the ISM and IGM in the evolution of galaxies. We demonstrate this by simulating the radio continuum and HI emission from local galaxies back to high redshifts. Our simulations show that the AA4 surveys will make it possible to trace the thermal and nonthermal processes of the ISM in galaxies that are analogs to M51 and NGC6946, traced in continuum beyond cosmic noon (z=2-3) and the gas content traced by HI beyond z=1. Both simulations and precursor observations indicate the importance of nonthermal feedback at cosmic noon.

AI.tldr: The paper explores how thermal and nonthermal processes (magnetic fields, cosmic rays) in the ISM/IGM affect galaxy evolution. Using simulations of radio continuum and HI emission from local to high-redshift galaxies, the authors demonstrate that SKA Observatory surveys (AA4) can trace these processes beyond cosmic noon (z=2-3) and gas content via HI beyond z=1, highlighting the importance of nonthermal feedback at cosmic noon.
AI.motivation: Investigating thermal and nonthermal processes in the ISM and IGM is vital for understanding galaxy evolution over cosmic time, as nonthermal processes (magnetic fields, cosmic rays) decelerate massive star formation and contribute to galactic winds/outflows, with stronger effects at higher redshifts.
AI.method: Simulating radio continuum and HI emission from local galaxies back to high redshifts to demonstrate the capabilities of SKA Observatory surveys (AA4) for tracing thermal and nonthermal ISM processes.
AI.result: AA4 surveys can trace thermal and nonthermal ISM processes in galaxies analogous to M51 and NGC6946 in continuum beyond cosmic noon (z=2-3) and HI gas content beyond z=1.
AI.conclusion: Both simulations and precursor observations indicate the importance of nonthermal feedback at cosmic noon, and the SKA Observatory will enable major breakthroughs in mapping these processes in distant universe galaxies.

title: Unveiling a cosmic tango: Integral field spectroscopy and numerical simulations of Arp 143's interaction
comment: Accepted for publication in MNRAS. 34 pages, 32 figures
summary: We present spectral data cubes of the interacting galaxy system Arp 143, composed of the ring galaxy NGC 2445 and the lenticular galaxy NGC 2444, obtained with the imaging Fourier transform spectrometer SITELLE at the Canada-France-Hawaii Telescope. Our data allow to probe the kinematics of the interaction and the chemical properties of the ionized gas. Star-forming regions are almost exclusively found in the ring and nucleus of NGC 2445 with the exception of a few very faint ones discovered at the base of the long tidal plume extending north of NGC 2444. Analysis of the Hα velocity map reveals strong non-circular flows in the ring of NGC 2445, which is expanding. Its nucleus is off-centered with respect to the ring. Oxygen abundance in the ring is on average slightly sub-solar whereas it is close to solar in the nucleus. Broad-band images obtained with the Dragonfly Telephoto array allow to identify the tenuous stellar counterpart of the radio tidal plume. The interaction between the two galaxies is simulated with a chemodynamical evolution code; these simulations suggest that Arp 143 has resulted from a head-on collision between a S0 and a Sc spiral galaxy following a flyby encounter that triggered the formation of the long plume from debris of the disk galaxy.

AI.tldr: This paper presents SITELLE spectral data cubes of the interacting galaxy system Arp 143 (ring galaxy NGC 2445 and lenticular NGC 2444), revealing kinematics, chemical properties, and star formation patterns. Hα velocity maps show non-circular expanding flows in the ring with an off-center nucleus. Oxygen abundance is slightly sub-solar in the ring and solar in the nucleus. Dragonfly images reveal the stellar tidal plume. Chemodynamical simulations suggest Arp 143 originated from a head-on collision between an S0 and a Sc spiral galaxy after a flyby encounter that created the long plume from disk debris.
AI.motivation: To probe the kinematics of the interaction and the chemical properties of the ionized gas in the Arp 143 interacting galaxy system.
AI.method: Imaging Fourier transform spectroscopy (SITELLE at CFHT), broad-band Dragonfly Telephoto array imaging, and chemodynamical evolution simulations.
AI.result: Star-forming regions are almost exclusively in the ring and nucleus of NGC 2445; Hα velocity maps show strong non-circular expanding flows in the ring with an off-centered nucleus; oxygen abundance is slightly sub-solar in the ring and solar in the nucleus; Dragonfly images reveal the tenuous stellar tidal plume; simulations indicate a head-on collision between S0 and Sc spiral galaxies following a flyby encounter.
AI.conclusion: Arp 143 likely formed from a head-on collision between an S0 galaxy (NGC 2444) and an Sc spiral galaxy (NGC 2445) after a flyby encounter that produced the long tidal plume from the spiral's debris.

title: Start of orbit librations and the bar growth timescale
comment: 13 pages, 12 figures
summary: We study a dynamical model of the Galaxy with an analytical bar that reproduces the radial velocity $V_R$ profiles as a function of the Galactocentric distance $R$ obtained from the Gaia DR3 data. The model radial velocity profiles show a periodic increase in $V_R$ caused by orbits trapped into libration near the outer Lindblad resonance (OLR). To determine the moment when the librations start, we built a set of additional models differing only in the bar growth time $T_g$. The temporal dependences of the radial velocity $V_R$ in the models with different $T_g$ retain their shape but are shifted relative to each other in time $t$. The shift providing the best agreement between the model dependences is proportional to $T_g$ with the coefficient $k = 0.54 \pm 0.02$. Orbit librations do not start when the bar reaches its full strength, but when it attains only 54% of its maximum strength. Since the maximum bar strength in the models is $Q_b = 0.314$, the librations start when the bar strength reaches $Q_b = 0.170$.

AI.tldr: This paper studies a dynamical Galaxy model with an analytical bar that reproduces Gaia DR3 radial velocity profiles, finding that orbit librations near the outer Lindblad resonance (OLR) begin when the bar reaches 54% of its maximum strength ($Q_b = 0.170$), not when fully grown.
AI.motivation: To understand when orbit librations near the outer Lindblad resonance (OLR) begin during bar growth, as this determines the timing of periodic radial velocity increases observed in Gaia DR3 data.
AI.method: Constructed a dynamical Galaxy model with an analytical bar matching Gaia DR3 $V_R(R)$ profiles; built additional models varying only the bar growth time $T_g$; analyzed temporal shifts in radial velocity profiles to determine the onset of orbit librations.
AI.result: The shift providing best agreement between model dependences is proportional to $T_g$ with coefficient $k = 0.54 \pm 0.02$, indicating librations start when bar reaches 54% of its maximum strength, corresponding to $Q_b = 0.170$.
AI.conclusion: Orbit librations near the OLR do not begin when the bar reaches full strength but when it attains 54% of its maximum strength ($Q_b = 0.170$), which determines the onset of periodic radial velocity increases in the Galaxy.

title: Probing Anomalous Microwave Emission with the Square Kilometre Array
comment: Published in Advancing Astrophysics with the SKAII(AASKAII), 2026 (arXiv:2606.20366). Report-no: AASKAII/Vidal01
summary: Anomalous microwave emission (AME) represents an excess of radiation in the 10-60 GHz range, distinct from synchrotron, free-free, or thermal dust emission. Although most commonly attributed to electric dipole radiation from rapidly rotating small dust grains (spinning dust), alternative mechanisms such as magnetic dipole emission (MDE) remain plausible. The detection of AME across diverse environments, from diffuse interstellar clouds to protoplanetary disks and external galaxies, suggests that multiple physical processes or carriers may contribute to its origin. Understanding AME is essential for both Galactic astrophysics and cosmology, as it constitutes a significant foreground for cosmic microwave background (CMB) studies, potentially biasing measurements. This chapter reviews current theoretical frameworks and observational evidence for AME, highlighting the key outstanding questions concerning its emission mechanisms, carriers, and polarization properties. We discuss how the Square Kilometre Array Observatory (SKAO), through its unprecedented sensitivity, angular resolution, and frequency coverage, will transform AME studies. SKA observations will enable detailed mapping of AME morphology, precise characterisation of its spectral energy distribution, and the identification of its carriers in Galactic and extragalactic environments. By combining SKA-mid data with higher-frequency observations from ALMA and other facilities such as SPHEREx, it will be possible to disentangle competing models and exploit AME as a diagnostic probe of interstellar grain physics and the small-scale structure of the interstellar medium.

AI.tldr: Anomalous microwave emission (AME) is an excess radiation (10-60 GHz) likely due to spinning dust or magnetic dipole emission, significant as a CMB foreground. The SKA Observatory will revolutionize AME studies by mapping morphology, characterizing SEDs, and identifying carriers, especially when combined with ALMA and SPHEREx.
AI.motivation: AME is a poorly understood emission component that constitutes a significant foreground for CMB cosmology, potentially biasing measurements; understanding its origin is essential for both Galactic astrophysics and accurate CMB analysis.
AI.method: The chapter reviews current theoretical frameworks (spinning dust, magnetic dipole emission) and observational evidence for AME, then discusses how SKAO's sensitivity, resolution, and frequency coverage—combined with ALMA and SPHEREx—will enable detailed mapping, SED characterization, and carrier identification.
AI.result: AME is detected across diverse environments (diffuse clouds, protoplanetary disks, external galaxies), but its emission mechanisms, carriers, and polarization properties remain unresolved. SKA-mid data synergized with ALMA and SPHEREx will disentangle competing models.
AI.conclusion: The SKA Observatory will transform AME studies by enabling precise characterization of its properties and carriers, allowing AME to be used as a diagnostic probe of interstellar grain physics and small-scale ISM structure.

title: HALO II: Constraining Hubble constant $H_{0}$ through continuum delay fitting of Fairall 9
comment: Submitted to A&A, 19 pages, 11 figures, and 2 tables
summary: The Hubble tension remains one of the most significant unresolved problems in modern cosmology. A key question is whether it may arise from underestimated systematic uncertainties in the different measurement techniques. In this context, new independent methods are of exceptional importance. We therefore pursue a novel approach to determining the Hubble constant, $H_{0}$ based on continuum time delay and spectral energy distribution (SED) modeling in active galactic nuclei (AGNs). Unlike conventional techniques, this method is entirely independent of the cosmic distance ladder and does not require cross-calibration against other distance indicators. As a result, it enables a direct determination of $H_{0}$, free from the arbitrary normalizations that often affect indirect measurements. We conducted a dedicated monitoring campaign of the Seyfert galaxy Fairall 9 and further developed the {\tt H0RIZON-AGN} model to interpret the resulting observations. The model incorporates the effects of radiation reprocessing in the surrounding cold accretion disk, enabling a more realistic description of the observed continuum delays. Through the simultaneous modeling of the continuum lag-spectrum and the broadband SED of Fairall 9, we derived a Hubble constant of $H_{0}=72.4_{-3.7}^{+3.4} \, \rm km \, s^{-1} \, Mpc^{-1}$. Achieving a measurement precision of approximately 5% from a single source demonstrates the considerable potential of this method for independent determinations of the Hubble constant. Our determination of $H_{0}$ is broadly consistent, within the current uncertainties, with both early- and late-Universe measurements. Future applications of the method to larger datasets, particularly those provided by the Vera Rubin Observatory, are expected to reduce the uncertainty to below 1%, thereby establishing this approach as a powerful independent probe of the Hubble tension.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a novel method to measure the Hubble constant $H_0$ using continuum time delays and SED modeling in AGNs, independent of the cosmic distance ladder. Monitoring the Seyfert galaxy Fairall 9 and using the H0RIZON-AGN model yields $H_0 = 72.4^{+3.4}_{-3.7} \, \rm km \, s^{-1} \, Mpc^{-1}$ (~5% precision). The method shows promise for sub-1% precision with future surveys like the Vera Rubin Observatory, offering a new independent probe of the Hubble tension.
AI.motivation: The Hubble tension—a discrepancy between early- and late-Universe $H_0$ measurements—remains unresolved. The authors aim to develop a new, independent method for determining $H_0$ that avoids systematic uncertainties inherent in the cosmic distance ladder and cross-calibration dependencies.
AI.method: The method combines continuum time-delay (lag-spectrum) measurements and broadband SED modeling in AGNs, using the reprocessing of radiation in the cold accretion disk. The H0RIZON-AGN model interprets the observations, and a dedicated monitoring campaign of the Seyfert galaxy Fairall 9 was conducted to obtain the data.
AI.result: From a single source (Fairall 9), the authors derive $H_0 = 72.4^{+3.4}_{-3.7} \, \rm km \, s^{-1} \, Mpc^{-1}$, achieving ~5% precision. The result is consistent with both early- and late-Universe measurements within current uncertainties.
AI.conclusion: The method demonstrates significant potential as an independent probe of the Hubble tension. With larger datasets (e.g., from the Vera Rubin Observatory), the uncertainty is expected to drop below 1%, enabling a powerful test of the Hubble tension free from distance ladder systematics.

title: 3D Magnetic Field Vectors in Space: Bubbles, Clouds, and Filaments
comment: Published in Advancing Astrophysics with the SKA II (AASKAII), 2026 (arXiv:2606.20366). Report-no:AASKAII/Tahani01. Advancing Astrophysics with the SKA II (AASKAII) outlines the transformative scientific advances that will be enabled by the SKA telescopes. 30 pages, 5 figures
summary: Magnetic fields play important roles in the star-formation process across different spatial scales. The interplay between magnetic field strength (a key component of the interstellar medium's energy budget) and field orientation relative to density structures impacts how interstellar material evolves toward star formation. To understand galactic evolution toward stars, planets, and ultimately life, we need to map three-dimensional (3D) magnetic field vectors in 3D space. However, determining full vector information remains challenging due to projection effects and the complex relationship between observable tracers and field geometry. We outline the observational techniques that can be used to probe the 3D magnetic field structures of objects such as supernova remnants (SNR), superbubbles, HII regions, and HI filaments in the diffuse interstellar medium (ISM), and objects in the dense ISM such as molecular clouds, filaments, and cores. The main SKA-specific observational techniques include synchrotron emission and Faraday rotation of both compact sources and the diffuse emission. We discuss how SKA AA4 will allow implementation of the techniques we describe, leveraging the vastly improved sensitivity, resolution and uv-coverage compared to existing datasets. This will enhance our ability to reconstruct 3D magnetic field vectors, advancing our understanding of magnetic fields in Galactic evolution and star formation.

AI.tldr: This paper discusses observational techniques for mapping 3D magnetic field vectors in the interstellar medium using SKA AA4, leveraging synchrotron emission and Faraday rotation to overcome projection effects and improve understanding of magnetic fields in star formation and Galactic evolution.
AI.motivation: Understanding the role of magnetic fields in star formation requires full 3D vector information, but projection effects and complex tracer-field relationships make this challenging to obtain.
AI.method: The paper outlines observational techniques for probing 3D magnetic fields across different ISM environments (SNRs, superbubbles, HII regions, HI filaments, molecular clouds, filaments, cores), focusing on synchrotron emission and Faraday rotation from compact sources and diffuse emission, enabled by SKA AA4's improved sensitivity, resolution, and uv-coverage.
AI.result: SKA AA4 will significantly enhance the ability to reconstruct 3D magnetic field vectors across diverse Galactic environments by overcoming limitations of existing datasets.
AI.conclusion: Leveraging SKA AA4's advanced capabilities will advance our understanding of magnetic fields in Galactic evolution and star formation by enabling full 3D magnetic field vector reconstruction.
